card.chief_complaint: brief loss of consciousness in bathroom after urination

ask.changes_what: Typical prodrome + trigger, no heart disease, normal ECG: reflex syncope likely, limit testing. No prodrome, especially with heart disease or abnormal ECG: pursue cardiac evaluation/monitoring.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use a reassuring prodrome to forgo ECG or to dismiss syncope in a patient with structural heart disease, exertional or supine syncope, or a family history of sudden death.
ask.escalation_warning: Syncope without prodrome plus heart disease, abnormal ECG, palpitations, exertional or supine occurrence warrants monitored cardiac evaluation.

evidence.target_condition: Vasovagal syncope (Calgary Syncope Symptom Score, composite history score incorporating prodromal items)

evidence.reference_standard: Final diagnosis of cardiac vs non-cardiac syncope in each source study

evidence.citation: Berecki-Gisolf J, Sheldon A, Wieling W, et al. Identifying cardiac syncope based on clinical history: a literature-based model tested in four independent datasets. PLoS One. 2013;8(9):e75255.

evidence.reference_standard: Final diagnosis of cardiac vs non-cardiac syncope in each source study
evidence.target_condition: Cardiac syncope (prodromal nausea)

ask.how: Ask the patient (and any witness) what they felt in the seconds to minutes before losing consciousness: nausea, warmth, sweating, visual graying, feeling cold, headache; and what they were doing (standing long, micturition, cough, pain, after a meal). Ask about mood or behaviour change before and after the event and how long the warning lasted.
ask.negative_finding: Absent or very brief prodrome modestly raises the likelihood of cardiac syncope (LR about 1.7 in pooled derivation data) but is common in older patients with reflex syncope, so it does not rule cardiac causes in or out.
ask.pitfalls: Older adults with vasovagal syncope often report no prodrome and have amnesia for the event; prodrome duration and quality are poorly recalled without a witness. Arrhythmic syncope can be preceded by palpitations or brief lightheadedness that patients call a 'prodrome'.
ask.positive_finding: A typical autonomic prodrome with a situational trigger favours reflex (vasovagal/situational) syncope; individual prodromal features such as feeling cold, headache or mood change carry LRs of about 0.1-0.2 for cardiac syncope. A quantified history score (Calgary) diagnoses vasovagal syncope with sensitivity 89% and specificity 91%.
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to recall the event; witness account improves accuracy.
ask.title: Prodrome before loss of consciousness (nausea, warmth, diaphoresis, visual graying) and situational trigger (micturition, cough, prolonged standing, pain, post-prandial) vs none

ask.changes_what: Determines which bedside exam follows: HINTS for continuous spontaneous, Dix-Hallpike for triggered episodic, orthostatic vitals for standing-triggered, ECG/monitoring for spontaneous episodic.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use a reassuring timing/trigger pattern alone to exclude stroke in patients with vascular risk factors, new headache/neck pain, or any brainstem symptom; obtain the targeted examination.
ask.escalation_warning: Acute continuous dizziness with any of diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, limb ataxia, new deafness or inability to walk unaided is a stroke pathway until proven otherwise; up to 20% of early DWI-MRI are false negative.

evidence.citation: Herr RD, Zun L, Mathews JJ. A directed approach to the dizzy patient. Ann Emerg Med. 1989;18(6):664-672.
evidence.population: 125 ED patients with dizziness evaluated with a standardized 66-item history/exam/lab protocol
evidence.quote: The best predictors, either older age, lack of vertigo, or neurologic deficit, could identify 86% of "serious" dizziness with 42% specificity.
evidence.reference_standard: Emergency physician diagnosis modified by 1-month follow-up using predefined diagnostic criteria
evidence.target_condition: 'Serious' cause of dizziness (stroke/TIA, arrhythmia, medication, seizure, other requiring admission) - composite predictor: older age OR lack of vertigo OR neurologic deficit

ask.how: Instead of asking 'what kind of dizziness', ask: Is it there now continuously or does it come in discrete episodes? How long do episodes last (seconds, minutes, hours)? Is it brought on only by a trigger (head/position change, standing) or does it arise spontaneously? Then ask about diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, new hearing loss, headache or neck pain.
ask.negative_finding: A clear positional trigger with seconds-long episodes and no neurologic symptoms makes central causes unlikely, but isolated dizziness can still be a vertebrobasilar stroke.
ask.pitfalls: Symptom-quality descriptors (vertigo vs lightheadedness) are unreliable: 52% of ED patients changed their descriptor on retest after ~6 minutes, so do not triage on 'type'. Do not confuse 'worse with movement' (most vestibular causes) with 'only occurs with movement' (true trigger).
ask.positive_finding: Continuous acute vestibular syndrome demands HINTS-type eye examination for stroke; triggered brief episodes point to BPPV or orthostatic hypotension (test with Dix-Hallpike or orthostatic vitals); spontaneous episodes lasting minutes-hours suggest TIA, Meniere or arrhythmia. Any associated brainstem symptom raises stroke probability.
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to give a history; screen for red-flag neurologic symptoms before deciding on examination pathway.
ask.title: Timing and triggers (TiTrATE: episodic vs continuous, triggered vs spontaneous) rather than symptom quality; associated diplopia/dysarthria/dysphagia/hearing loss

ask.changes_what: Positive (prolonged confusion, lateral tongue bite): pursue seizure work-up (EEG, imaging). Negative with rapid reorientation: pursue syncope pathway (ECG, orthostatics, cardiac risk).
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on these features alone in patients with focal deficits, head injury, or possible nonconvulsive status; absence of tongue biting never excludes seizure.
ask.escalation_warning: Prolonged post-event confusion with fever, headache, focal signs, or no return to baseline needs urgent evaluation for structural, infectious, or ongoing seizure causes.

evidence.citation: Brigo F, Nardone R, Bongiovanni LG. Value of tongue biting in the differential diagnosis between epileptic seizures and syncope. Seizure. 2012;21(8):568-572.
evidence.population: Pooled: 75 patients with epileptic seizures and 98 with syncope from 2 studies
evidence.quote: sensitivity 33%, specificity 96%, pLR 8.167 (95% CI 2.969-22.461) and nLR 0.695 (95% CI 0.589-0.82)
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical/video-EEG diagnosis of epileptic seizure vs syncope as defined in the included studies
evidence.target_condition: Epileptic seizure (vs syncope) - finding: tongue biting (any)

evidence.citation: Benbadis SR, Wolgamuth BR, Goren H, Brener S, Fouad-Tarazi F. Value of tongue biting in the diagnosis of seizures. Arch Intern Med. 1995;155(21):2346-2349.
evidence.population: 63 epilepsy-monitoring-unit patients with bilateral motor activity and/or complete LOC (34 epileptic, 29 nonepileptic) plus 45 patients with syncope (retrospective)
evidence.quote: Tongue biting had a sensitivity of 24% and a specificity of 99% for the diagnosis of generalized tonic-clonic seizures.
evidence.reference_standard: Video-EEG monitoring (epilepsy monitoring unit); syncope by clinical diagnosis
evidence.target_condition: Generalized tonic-clonic seizure (vs nonepileptic events and syncope) - finding: tongue biting

evidence.citation: Hoefnagels WA, Padberg GW, Overweg J, van der Velde EA, Roos RA. Transient loss of consciousness: the value of the history for distinguishing seizure from syncope. J Neurol. 1991;238(1):39-43.
evidence.population: 94 consecutive patients aged 15+ with transient loss of consciousness (41 seizure, 53 syncope)
evidence.quote: We found a seizure five times more likely than syncope if the patient was disoriented after the event
evidence.reference_standard: Eyewitness-observed clonic movements or automatisms classified the event as a seizure
evidence.target_condition: Seizure (vs syncope) - finding: disorientation immediately after the event (eyewitness report)

evidence.citation: Sheldon R, Rose S, Ritchie D, et al. Historical criteria that distinguish syncope from seizures. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2002;40(1):142-148.
evidence.population: 539 patients with loss of consciousness of known cause (102 seizures; 437 syncope incl. 267 tilt-positive vasovagal, 90 VT, 80 other)
evidence.quote: The point score based on symptoms alone correctly classified 94% of patients, diagnosing seizures with 94% sensitivity and 94% specificity.
evidence.reference_standard: Established cause of LOC (tilt testing, electrophysiology, EEG/clinical epilepsy diagnosis); split-half validation
evidence.target_condition: Seizure (vs syncope) - COMPOSITE Calgary historical point score (includes post-event confusion, tongue biting, head turning, incontinence items), not a single feature

ask.how: Take the history from an eyewitness where possible. Ask how long the patient was confused or disoriented after coming round (seconds vs many minutes), whether the tongue was bitten and where (lateral border vs tip), whether the head or eyes turned to one side, and whether there was incontinence. Inspect the lateral tongue for laceration.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of tongue biting barely lowers seizure probability (pooled LR- 0.70, sensitivity ~0.24-0.33). Rapid, full orientation on waking favours syncope.
ask.pitfalls: Brief myoclonic jerks and even a few seconds of confusion are common in convulsive syncope; incontinence and injury did not discriminate in Hoefnagels 1991. Tip-of-tongue bites occur in syncope.
ask.positive_finding: Disorientation after the event made seizure about five times more likely than syncope (Hoefnagels 1991); tongue biting is highly specific for generalised seizure (pooled LR+ 8.2, spec 0.96), and lateral tongue biting was 100% specific in Benbadis 1995.
ask.prerequisites: An eyewitness account materially improves accuracy; the patient's own recall of the event is often absent.
ask.title: Seizure-vs-syncope features: prolonged (>1-5 min) post-event confusion, lateral tongue biting, head turning, incontinence

ask.changes_what: Positive: treat as significant volume loss - IV access, fluid/blood, search for bleeding source; negative: does not exclude moderate haemorrhage, use labs/other findings.
ask.contraindications: Do not stand a patient who is already hypotensive, in shock, or with suspected unstable spine/pelvic injury.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not attempt standing in patients who are hypotensive supine, obtunded, or at high fall risk; do not apply the volunteer-derived numbers uncritically to elderly patients on antihypertensives, beta-blockers or with autonomic neuropathy.
ask.escalation_warning: Inability to stand because of dizziness in a patient with suspected bleeding indicates large-volume loss: obtain large-bore access, type and crossmatch, and escalate immediately.

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing phlebotomy (pooled RCE analysis of postural vital-sign studies)
evidence.quote: a much greater sensitivity for large blood loss of 97% (95% CI, 91%-100%); the corresponding specificity is 98% (95% CI, 97%-99%)
evidence.reference_standard: Known volume of blood removed by phlebotomy (before vs after)
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolaemia from LARGE acute blood loss (630-1150 mL) - finding: severe postural dizziness (preventing upright vitals) OR postural pulse increment >=30/min

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing phlebotomy (pooled RCE analysis of postural vital-sign studies)
evidence.quote: The presence of either finding has a sensitivity for moderate blood loss of only 22% (95% confidence interval [CI], 6%-48%)
evidence.reference_standard: Known volume of blood removed by phlebotomy (before vs after)
evidence.target_condition: Hypovolaemia from MODERATE acute blood loss (450-630 mL) - finding: severe postural dizziness OR postural pulse increment >=30/min

ask.how: After supine vitals, stand the patient (with assistance) and ask about dizziness while measuring pulse and BP at about 1 minute. 'Severe' means dizziness so marked the patient cannot stay standing long enough for upright vitals or nearly faints; record it as a positive finding in its own right, together with any pulse increment of 30/min or more.
ask.negative_finding: Absence is reassuring only against large blood loss (sensitivity 0.97); after moderate (450-630 mL) loss the finding is usually absent (sensitivity 0.22), so a negative test does not exclude clinically important haemorrhage.
ask.pitfalls: Mild postural dizziness has no proven diagnostic value; supine tachycardia or hypotension is often absent even after 1 L loss. Evidence comes from healthy volunteers after phlebotomy, not from elderly or medicated ED patients, in whom baseline orthostatic symptoms are common.
ask.positive_finding: Severe postural dizziness (or a postural pulse increment >=30/min) is highly specific (0.98) for hypovolaemia from blood loss and is present in almost all subjects after large (630-1150 mL) blood loss.
ask.prerequisites: Supine rest for at least 2 minutes before standing; an assistant to prevent a fall. Sitting is not an adequate substitute for standing.
ask.title: Severe postural dizziness / inability to stand for vitals

examine.changes_what: Positive: treat as significant hypovolemia/bleeding or medication-related OH and act; negative: large blood loss unlikely, but moderate loss still possible.
examine.contraindications: Do not stand a patient who is frankly hypotensive, has an unstable spine/pelvis, or cannot safely bear weight.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not attempt standing measurements in a patient who is already hypotensive, too dizzy or weak to stand safely, or has an unstable spine or pelvis; a patient too dizzy to stand counts as a positive test.
examine.escalation_warning: A positive test in a patient with possible bleeding indicates large volume loss and should trigger resuscitation and source search, not observation.

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy (pooled from volunteer studies)
evidence.quote: a much greater sensitivity for large blood loss of 97% (95% CI, 91%-100%); the corresponding specificity is 98% (95% CI, 97%-99%)
evidence.reference_standard: Known volume of phlebotomy
evidence.target_condition: Large acute blood loss (630-1150 mL) - postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy (pooled from volunteer studies)
evidence.quote: has a sensitivity for moderate blood loss of only 22% (95% confidence interval [CI], 6%-48%)
evidence.reference_standard: Known volume of phlebotomy
evidence.target_condition: Moderate acute blood loss (450-630 mL) - postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness

evidence.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
evidence.population: Healthy adult volunteers undergoing controlled phlebotomy
evidence.quote: Supine hypotension and tachycardia are frequently absent, even after up to 1150 mL of blood loss (sensitivity, 33%; 95% CI, 21%-47%, for supine hypotension)
evidence.reference_standard: Known volume of phlebotomy
evidence.target_condition: Blood loss up to 1150 mL - supine hypotension (comparator finding, not postural)

examine.how: Measure BP and pulse after >=2 min supine, then have the patient stand and repeat at 1 and 3 min (standing, not sitting). Record SBP fall >=20 or DBP fall >=10 mmHg, pulse rise >=30/min, and whether the patient is too dizzy to stand (count that as positive).
examine.negative_finding: A normal postural pulse response argues strongly against large blood loss (LR- about 0.03) but misses most moderate (450-630 mL) losses (sensitivity 22%). Normal orthostatics do not exclude hypovolemia from vomiting/diarrhea.
examine.pitfalls: Supine hypotension and tachycardia are frequently absent even after 1 L blood loss. Beta-blockers blunt the pulse response; sitting instead of standing lowers sensitivity; mild postural dizziness alone has no proven value.
examine.positive_finding: A postural pulse increment >=30/min or severe postural dizziness is highly specific (98%) for blood loss and is nearly always present after large (>1 L) hemorrhage. In an older patient with syncope, an SBP fall >=20 mmHg reproducing symptoms supports orthostatic hypotension, though asymptomatic falls are common with age and medications.
examine.prerequisites: Automated or manual cuff, an assistant to steady the patient, supine rest of at least 2 minutes first.
examine.title: Orthostatic vitals: SBP drop >=20 / DBP >=10 mmHg or pulse increment >=30/min at 1-3 min standing

examine.changes_what: Positive: treat as UGIB (IV access, type and screen, PPI, early endoscopy, Glasgow-Blatchford risk stratification); clots or bright red blood redirect to a lower source.
examine.contraindications: Relative: severe neutropenia, recent anorectal surgery, or patient refusal; never delay resuscitation for the exam.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of melena to exclude significant bleeding in a hypotensive or syncopal patient, or attribute black stool to bleeding without excluding iron/bismuth.
examine.escalation_warning: Melena with tachycardia, hypotension, hemoglobin <8 g/dL, cirrhosis or anticoagulation indicates severe UGIB: two large-bore IVs, blood products, urgent GI endoscopy and monitored bed.

evidence.citation: Srygley FD, Gerardo CJ, Tran T, Fisher DA. Does this patient have a severe upper gastrointestinal bleed? JAMA. 2012;307(10):1072-1079.
evidence.population: Adults admitted or evaluated in ED with acute GI bleeding (8 studies of UGIB vs LGIB; N=1776)
evidence.quote: melenic stool on examination (LR, 25; 95% CI, 4-174)
evidence.reference_standard: Endoscopic localization of bleeding source
evidence.target_condition: Upper GI bleeding (vs lower GI source); finding = melenic stool on examination

evidence.citation: Srygley FD, Gerardo CJ, Tran T, Fisher DA. Does this patient have a severe upper gastrointestinal bleed? JAMA. 2012;307(10):1072-1079.
evidence.location: Abstract, Results (reported as a range across studies, 5.1-5.9, not a CI; lower bound entered as value)
evidence.population: Adults with acute GI bleeding, studies of UGIB vs LGIB localization
evidence.quote: a patient-reported history of melena (LR range, 5.1-5.9)
evidence.reference_standard: Endoscopic localization of bleeding source
evidence.target_condition: Upper GI bleeding (vs lower GI source); finding = patient-reported history of melena

evidence.citation: Srygley FD, Gerardo CJ, Tran T, Fisher DA. Does this patient have a severe upper gastrointestinal bleed? JAMA. 2012;307(10):1072-1079.
evidence.location: Abstract, Results (LR for presence of clots, i.e. finding present argues against UGIB)
evidence.population: Adults with acute GI bleeding, studies of UGIB vs LGIB localization
evidence.quote: the presence of blood clots in stool (LR, 0.05; 95% CI, 0.01-0.38) decreases the likelihood of a UGIB
evidence.reference_standard: Endoscopic localization of bleeding source
evidence.target_condition: Upper GI bleeding (vs lower GI source); finding = blood clots in stool (present)

examine.how: Ask about black, tarry, sticky, foul-smelling stool and any hematemesis or coffee-ground emesis, and about iron, bismuth or recent NSAID/anticoagulant use. Perform a digital rectal exam and inspect the glove: melena is black, tarry and glistening; distinguish from formed dark stool and from red blood or clots.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of melena does not exclude UGIB (brisk bleeds present as hematochezia); blood clots in stool argue against an upper source (LR 0.05).
examine.pitfalls: Iron and bismuth cause black non-tarry stool; melena requires roughly 50 mL of blood and ~8 h of transit, so early or very brisk bleeds may not yet show it. Melena localizes the source but does not by itself grade severity.
examine.positive_finding: Melenic stool on examination strongly indicates an upper GI source (LR 25), and reported melena moderately so (LR 5.1-5.9); in a patient with syncope or hypotension it establishes hemorrhage as the likely cause.
examine.prerequisites: Patient consent and privacy; gloves; adequate light to inspect stool colour.
examine.title: Melena on digital rectal exam, or reported black tarry stool / hematemesis

examine.changes_what: Positive with symptom reproduction in unexplained syncope/falls: cardioinhibitory type -> pacing evaluation; negative supine+upright: remove CSS from the differential, pursue tilt/monitoring.
examine.contraindications: Carotid bruit; TIA or stroke within 3 months; myocardial infarction within 3 months; known carotid stenosis; prior carotid surgery is a relative contraindication. Never massage both sides simultaneously.
examine.do_not_use_when: Carotid bruit, carotid stenosis or endarterectomy, TIA/stroke or MI within 3 months, ventricular tachycardia history; not without ECG and BP monitoring.
examine.escalation_warning: Prolonged asystole (>6 s) or hypotension with syncope during the test is a positive result but needs immediate supine positioning and readiness for atropine; any new focal neurological symptom after massage is a stroke until proven otherwise.

evidence.citation: Kerr SR, Pearce MS, Brayne C, Davis RJ, Kenny RA. Carotid sinus hypersensitivity in asymptomatic older persons: implications for diagnosis of syncope and falls. Arch Intern Med 2006;166:515-520.
evidence.population: 272 randomly sampled community residents >65 y (unselected for symptoms), UK general practice register
evidence.quote: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity was present in 107 individuals (39%); 24% had asystole of 3 seconds or greater during carotid sinus massage
evidence.reference_standard: No reference standard for carotid sinus syndrome; positive rate in an unselected community sample used as false-positive rate
evidence.target_condition: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity response (asystole >=3 s and/or SBP fall >=50 mmHg) - specificity estimated from positive rate in unselected community elders

evidence.citation: Kerr SR, Pearce MS, Brayne C, Davis RJ, Kenny RA. Carotid sinus hypersensitivity in asymptomatic older persons: implications for diagnosis of syncope and falls. Arch Intern Med 2006;166:515-520.
evidence.population: 80 community elders >65 y with no history of syncope, dizziness or falls
evidence.quote: In 80 previously asymptomatic individuals, carotid sinus hypersensitivity was present in 28 (35%) and accompanied by symptoms in 10.
evidence.reference_standard: No reference standard; positive rate in previously asymptomatic subsample used as false-positive rate
evidence.target_condition: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity response (asystole >=3 s and/or SBP fall >=50 mmHg) - specificity estimated from positive rate in elders with no history of syncope, dizziness or falls

evidence.citation: Kumar NP, Thomas A, Mudd P, Morris RO, Masud T. The usefulness of carotid sinus massage in different patient groups. Age Ageing 2004;33:159-163.
evidence.population: 44 asymptomatic controls >=60 y from a general practice register vs 221 symptomatic falls-clinic patients >60 y (130 unexplained syncope)
evidence.quote: we studied 44 asymptomatic control subjects and 221 symptomatic patients (130 with unexplained syncope, 41 with unexplained falls and 50 with unexplained dizziness)
evidence.reference_standard: No reference standard; asymptomatic controls used to estimate false-positive rate
evidence.target_condition: Carotid sinus syndrome response (asystole >3 s and/or SBP fall >50 mmHg, supine then upright) - specificity from asymptomatic controls; yield in unexplained syncope 22.3%

examine.how: With continuous ECG and beat-to-beat BP, firmly massage one carotid sinus (at the angle of the jaw, anterior to sternocleidomastoid) for 5-10 s; repeat on the other side, then repeat both sides at 60-70 degrees upright on a tilt table. Positive: asystole >=3 s and/or SBP fall >=50 mmHg, ideally with symptom reproduction.
examine.negative_finding: No pause and no significant BP fall in both supine and upright positions makes carotid sinus syndrome unlikely; a normal supine test alone is insufficient because many responses are only seen upright.
examine.pitfalls: A hypersensitive response is common in asymptomatic older people (39% of an unselected community sample >65 y), so a positive test without symptom reproduction should not stop the search for other causes; the vasodepressor component is missed without beat-to-beat BP.
examine.positive_finding: Asystole >=3 s (cardioinhibitory), SBP drop >=50 mmHg (vasodepressor) or both (mixed) supports carotid sinus hypersensitivity; the diagnosis of carotid sinus syndrome additionally requires reproduction of spontaneous symptoms.
examine.prerequisites: Continuous ECG monitoring and beat-to-beat (phasic) BP; auscultate both carotids first; resuscitation drugs/atropine and a tilt table for the upright phase; performed by trained staff.
examine.title: Carotid sinus massage 5-10 s each side, supine then upright, with continuous BP/pulse; contraindicated with bruit, TIA/stroke or MI within 3 months

examine.changes_what: Positive: pursue POTS work-up and exclude secondary causes (volume, thyroid, anemia, drugs); negative: redirect toward orthostatic hypotension, arrhythmia or vasovagal mechanisms.
examine.contraindications: Inability to stand safely, symptomatic hypotension or active bleeding/sepsis where orthostatic stress is unsafe; stop if syncope is imminent.
examine.do_not_use_when: Patient cannot stand safely or is acutely hypotensive, bleeding or septic; the test does not replace evaluation for arrhythmia or structural heart disease in exertional or unexplained syncope.
examine.escalation_warning: Standing-induced syncope with injury risk, or HR rise with hypotension in an acutely ill patient, indicates volume loss/sepsis/bleeding rather than POTS and needs urgent evaluation.

evidence.citation: Plash WB, Diedrich A, Biaggioni I, Garland EM, Paranjape SY, Black BK, et al. Diagnosing postural tachycardia syndrome: comparison of tilt testing compared with standing haemodynamics. Clin Sci (Lond). 2013.
evidence.population: 15 adults with previously diagnosed POTS vs 15 healthy controls (case-control), autonomic dysfunction center
evidence.quote: Sn (sensitivity) of the 30 bpm criterion was similar for all tests (TILT10=93%, STAND10=87%, TILT30=100%, and STAND30=93%).
evidence.reference_standard: Prior clinical diagnosis of POTS (sustained HR rise >=30 bpm with orthostatic symptoms, no orthostatic hypotension) vs healthy volunteer status
evidence.target_condition: Postural tachycardia syndrome (adults)

evidence.citation: Stewart JM, Medow MS. Can standing replace upright tilt table testing in the diagnosis of postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS) in the young? Clin Auton Res. 2025.
evidence.population: 36 adolescents (12.2-18.8 y) with tilt-defined POTS vs 39 healthy volunteers (13.1-18.9 y), case-control
evidence.quote: For 5 min stand ROC threshold was 26 beats per min (bpm), sensitivity of 70.6%, and specificity of 68.2%
evidence.reference_standard: POTS defined by orthostatic intolerance plus sustained excessive tachycardia without hypotension during 70-degree head-up tilt
evidence.target_condition: Postural tachycardia syndrome (adolescents <19 years), 5-min active stand at ROC-optimal threshold 26 bpm

examine.how: After >=5 min supine rest record HR and BP, then have the patient stand still (unsupported, minimal movement) and record HR and BP at 1, 3, 5 and 10 min while asking about lightheadedness, palpitations, visual change and near-syncope. Note the maximum sustained HR rise above supine and whether SBP falls >=20 mmHg.
examine.negative_finding: HR rise <30 bpm without symptoms makes POTS unlikely on that occasion; an accompanying SBP fall >=20 mmHg points instead to orthostatic hypotension.
examine.pitfalls: Deconditioning, anemia, dehydration, fever, anxiety, hyperthyroidism and drugs (vasodilators, stimulants) produce secondary orthostatic tachycardia and must be excluded; a single test is poorly reproducible and tilt gives larger HR rises than active standing. Thresholds derived in small case-control samples overstate accuracy.
examine.positive_finding: Sustained HR increase >=30 bpm (>=40 bpm in patients aged 12-19) within 10 min of standing with reproduction of orthostatic symptoms and no orthostatic hypotension (SBP fall <20 mmHg), in a patient with >=3-6 months of symptoms, meets consensus POTS criteria.
examine.prerequisites: Off obvious confounders where possible (recent caffeine, beta-blocker timing, acute illness); adequate hydration status noted; a chair or bed behind the patient and an assistant for near-syncope.
examine.title: Supine-to-standing heart rate increment (>=30 bpm sustained within 10 min, POTS-style) with symptom reproduction on standing
